lesson.title: The Linux Bridge: A Software Switch for Namespaces
lesson.summary: A Linux bridge is a virtual layer-2 switch built into the kernel that lets many network namespaces or interfaces exchange frames as if they were all plugged into the same physical switch.
lesson.body:
A bridge, in general, is a device that connects two or more network segments at layer 2, learning which MAC address lives behind which port and forwarding frames only where they need to go, flooding a frame out every port only when it does not yet know where the destination lives. A physical Ethernet switch is essentially a multi-port bridge built in hardware. A Linux bridge is the same idea implemented in software, inside the kernel, and it is the natural next step once you have more than two network namespaces to connect.

A single veth pair works fine for connecting exactly two namespaces, as a direct virtual cable between them. But that does not scale: connecting five namespaces to each other with individual veth pairs would require ten separate cables and does not resemble how real networks are built. Instead, you create one Linux bridge, a virtual switch, and connect every namespace to it with its own veth pair, exactly the way real hosts connect to a physical switch rather than being wired directly to one another.

Building this looks like an extension of the namespace example: create the bridge, bring it up, then for each namespace create a veth pair, put one end inside the namespace, and attach the other end to the bridge as a port.

  ip link add br0 type bridge
  ip link set br0 up

  ip netns add ns1
  ip link add veth1 type veth peer name veth1-br
  ip link set veth1 netns ns1
  ip link set veth1-br master br0
  ip link set veth1-br up
  ip netns exec ns1 ip addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev veth1
  ip netns exec ns1 ip link set veth1 up

  ip netns add ns2
  ip link add veth2 type veth peer name veth2-br
  ip link set veth2 netns ns2
  ip link set veth2-br master br0
  ip link set veth2-br up
  ip netns exec ns2 ip addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev veth2
  ip netns exec ns2 ip link set veth2 up

Repeating the pattern for a third namespace, ns3 with address 10.0.0.3, gives you three isolated network namespaces that can all reach one another through br0, and the bridge itself behaves exactly like the general bridge concept: it learns which MAC address sits behind veth1-br, veth2-br, and veth3-br by observing traffic, and forwards frames accordingly rather than blindly flooding every frame everywhere once it has learned the topology. If you also attach the host's physical interface to the bridge and configure NAT, the namespaces can reach the outside network too.

This exact pattern, a network namespace per container plus a veth pair into a shared Linux bridge, is what Docker's default bridge network driver does automatically when you create containers without specifying custom networking: the bridge is usually named docker0, and every container you start gets its own namespace and its own veth port plugged into it, which is why containers on the same Docker host can reach each other by IP out of the box.
